titulo: Honest metrics: pass@k, pass^k, variance, SWE-bench, and METR
lead: "Gets 90% right" can mean it gets it right almost every time, or that it gets it right at least once in three tries. For a loop that runs without you, only the first one will do. In this lesson you measure both on your golden set, see how much the number swings between rounds, and learn to read SWE-bench and the METR horizon without overstating them.
objetivo: measure pass@k and pass^k with repetitions, read the variance between rounds, and cite SWE-bench and the METR horizon without overstating them.

aprende.t: pass@k (at least one hit) and pass^k (gets them all)
Repeat the set and watch the number swing
SWE-bench: passing the test is not being accepted
METR horizon: what it measures and what it doesn't

hero_alt: An oscilloscope screen with overlapping curves, and next to it graph paper with scattered dots.

secoes.titulo: The same agent, three different numbers

nos.detalhe: rodar-evals.py runs each case k times. An agent built on a language model doesn't always answer the same way: the same question can come out right once and wrong the next time.
The fraction of cases with at least one hit in k attempts. It's useful when someone picks the best of several outputs. It grows with k, and it's the number that looks good in the announcement.

The fraction of cases that got all k attempts right. This is what an unsupervised loop needs: nobody is going to pick the best one. It drops as k grows. With 75% per attempt, 3 independent attempts give about 42% (example from Anthropic's evals article).
The rate changes from round to round. A difference between two versions smaller than this swing is not an improvement: it's noise. Run more than once before you compare.

secoes.legenda: For an autonomous loop, report pass^k and the spread between rounds, not pass@k.

secoes.sub: The fake triage agent, with TRIAGEM_RUIDO=0.25, gets the "urgente" case wrong in 25% of attempts (fixed draw, reproducible).

abas.html:
10 casos × 3 tentativas
taxa por tentativa: 73%  (rodada 1: 70% · rodada 2: 80% · rodada 3: 70%; desvio 5 pontos)
pass@3: 90%  (ao menos 1 acerto)
pass^3: 50%  (acertou todas)
se fossem independentes, 73%^3 = 39%
instáveis: t01 t06 t08 t10

The same agent can be advertised as "90%" (pass@3) or described as "half the cases always come out right" (pass^3). Round 2 alone would say 80%; rounds 1 and 3, 70%.

pass^3 came out above the independent estimate (39%) because the errors aren't independent: 5 cases never fail and the trap case (t07) always fails. In your own set, the list of unstable cases is the list of cases to study first.

secoes.sub: Only what the primary source says, with a date.

texto: METR estimated that about half of the PRs that pass the SWE-bench Verified tests would not be accepted by the project's maintainers.
A green test measures what the test covers. Style, scope, and side effects are left out: that's the space for the skeptical evaluator and the human sample.

There are reports in secondary sources that public code benchmarks leaked into training data and that providers switched benchmarks because of it. We did not confirm the numbers in the primary source.
A practical consequence that doesn't depend on the number: your golden set, private and drawn from your own failures, tells you more about your agent than any public leaderboard.
The 50% horizon = the length of a task (in human expert time) that the model gets right half the time. It is not how long the agent works on its own.
The tasks are in software engineering, ML, and security, well specified and verifiable by code. It doesn't apply to a vague task.

METR's FAQ gives about 2 h 17 min for GPT-5. Claude Mythos Preview (early version, evaluated in March 2026) came in at at least 16 h, with a 95% interval of 8.5 h to 55 h, at the limit of what METR says it can measure.
The time horizons page has been retired: last model added on 05/08/2026, last notice on 09/08/2026. Later models have no official horizon. Use it as an order of magnitude, at 50% success, not 80%.

perguntas.p: For a loop that runs unsupervised, which metric matters?
opcoes: The total from the first round
perguntas.explica: Nobody picks the best of three in an autonomous loop: every run has to get it right. pass^k measures that.

perguntas.p: With 75% success per attempt, independent, what is pass^3?
perguntas.explica: 0.75 × 0.75 × 0.75 ≈ 0.42. The example is in Anthropic's evals article (01/09/2026).

perguntas.p: According to METR (03/10/2026), what happens to PRs that pass SWE-bench Verified?
opcoes: All of them would be accepted
About half would not be accepted by the maintainers
perguntas.explica: Passing the test is not being mergeable. The test covers part of what a maintainer requires.

perguntas.p: What does a 50% horizon of 16 h mean?
opcoes: The agent works 16 h on its own
Tasks that would take a specialist 16 h are solved half the time, in a well-specified set
The agent gets 50% of everything right in 16 h
The model has 16 h of context
perguntas.explica: It is the task duration measured in human time, at 50% success, on verifiable tasks. It is not autonomy, and it does not hold for vague tasks.

itens.texto: pass@k measures luck with choice; pass^k measures what happens when nobody chooses.
Run more than once; a difference smaller than the swing between rounds is not a gain.

itens.t: Benchmark with a date and a caveat
itens.texto: Passing SWE-bench is not being accepted; METR horizon is human task time at 50%, and the series stopped in 2026.
